desc:
The array nums contains positive integers. Every non-empty contiguous subarray has a sum; subarrays at different positions are counted separately even when their sums are equal. Sort all n(n+1)/2 sums in non-decreasing order and return the k-th one (1-indexed).

Example: for nums = [2, 1, 3] the subarray sums are 2, 1, 3, 3, 4, 6, sorted 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, so k = 4 gives 3.
hints: Generating all O(n<sup>2</sup>) sums and sorting them is too much memory for n = 5000 in many settings. Think about the answer as a value.
For a limit S, how many subarrays have sum at most S? All numbers are positive, so a sliding window with two pointers counts them in O(n).
Binary search the smallest S between min(nums) and sum(nums) with at least k subarrays of sum ≤ S.
editorial: Because all elements are positive, extending a subarray always increases its sum, which makes the counting step easy. For a fixed limit S, sweep right across the array, maintaining the window sum; shrink from the left while the sum exceeds S. Every start index in [left, right] gives a valid subarray ending at right, so add right - left + 1. That is count(S) in O(n).

count(S) is non-decreasing in S. The k-th smallest sum is the smallest S with count(S) ≥ k, and it is an actual subarray sum because count only increases at sums that exist. The search range is [min(nums), sum(nums)], at most about 5·107, so around 26 iterations.
Total time is O(n log(sum)) and space is O(1). Positivity is essential: with negative numbers the window sum is not monotone and the two-pointer count is invalid.
